author: Gary Franchi
title: REACTION: Student Loan Office Spinoff Plan Draws Fire and Praise as Musk Roadster News Lands | Next News Network
text:
The Education Department is planning to spin off its Federal Student Aid office into a new independent agency by October first, 2027, according to a report from The Washington Sun citing three sources familiar with the matter and internal documents. The claim, carried by the account @RedState in a post that described it as a "Good Start," set off a round of reaction from conservative commentators and news accounts across the platform, with the student loan overhaul drawing both praise and sharp criticism as details remained scarce.
According to the report, Richard Lucas, the office's chief operating officer, is spearheading the change alongside the White House's Office of Management and Budget. The plan would reshape how forty-five million borrowers repay the one point six trillion dollars currently in the Education Department's portfolio of outstanding debts, the report stated. It would also raise additional legal complications around the future of the department, an agency President Donald Trump and Secretary Linda McMahon have repeatedly said they want to eliminate entirely.
The reaction from @RedState was immediate and pointed. In its post, the account framed the move as a welcome first step, writing, "Good Start: Education Department Plans to Spin Off Student Loan Office by 2027." The post did not elaborate on what a fully spun-off agency would look like, and the underlying report acknowledged that details so far are scarce. What is clear, according to the report, is that repayment will still be expected.
The account's commentary, delivered alongside the news, took direct aim at borrowers who have argued the federal government should absorb the debt. "Over the years, I've challenged quite a few people to show me where the Constitution authorizes the federal government to handle, much less subsidize, student loans," the account wrote. "Nobody has ever given an answer other than a few half-hearted attempts at invoking 'promote the general welfare.'"
The post went further, criticizing borrowers who believe taxpayers should shoulder the burden. "Well, a significant number of those borrowers have the notion that the taxpayers should repay the $1.6 trillion in debts, despite the fact that these young skulls full of mush signed contracts, which they presumably read, including the section on repayment," the account wrote. The line drew attention for its blunt assessment, though the post itself offered no data to support the characterization of borrower sentiment.
Not everyone within the department is on board, according to the report. Some Education Department officials believe the administration is rushing the overhaul, the report stated, and they may be right. One of President Trump's second-term priorities was to shut down the department altogether, which the report described as "troublesome and likely unconstitutional." The tension between shutting the department down and standing up a new independent agency to handle its core function was left unresolved in the report.
As the student loan story circulated, another announcement landed in the same news cycle. The account @FirstSquawk posted that Elon Musk has announced plans to start Roadster production in 2028. The post, dated October sixteenth, 2026, offered no further details. The claim arrives after almost a decade of delays on the vehicle. Musk first debuted the Roadster refresh concept in 2017, according to other coverage of the subject, and Tesla has since missed every targeted delivery date. The announcement, as carried by @FirstSquawk, did not specify a location for production or a price point.
The two stories moved through separate audiences but landed on the same feeds. The @RedState post framed the student loan spinoff as a fiscal and constitutional matter, while the @FirstSquawk post offered a forward-looking product announcement with no immediate policy implications. Neither account provided additional sourcing for the claims in their posts beyond what was attributed.
The student loan report, as summarized by @RedState, noted that the new office's structure remains unclear. What is known, according to the report, is that the spinoff is targeted for October first, 2027, and that Lucas is working with the Office of Management and Budget to stand it up. The report described the effort as moving "rapidly," though it did not specify what steps have already been taken or what legal hurdles remain. The department has not publicly confirmed the plan, and the report relied on unnamed sources and internal documents.
For borrowers, the practical effect of the reported plan is uncertain. The report stated that repayment will still be expected, but it did not detail how the new agency would handle income-driven repayment plans, forgiveness programs, or servicing contracts. Those questions were left unanswered in the account carried by @RedState, which focused its commentary on the constitutional question and the burden on taxpayers rather than the mechanics of the transition.
The political context is significant. President Trump and Secretary McMahon have both publicly stated their desire to eliminate the Education Department entirely. Spinning off the student loan office could be a step toward that goal, or it could complicate it by creating a new entity that would need its own congressional authorization and oversight. The report noted that the plan "would also raise additional legal complications around the future of the department," though it did not specify what those complications might be.
The @RedState post did not address those complications directly. Instead, it returned to the constitutional argument that has animated conservative opposition to federal student lending for years. The account's challenge to readers — to show where the Constitution authorizes the federal government to handle or subsidize student loans — has been a recurring theme in conservative circles, though the report itself did not attempt to answer it.
Next News Network could not independently verify the claims that the Education Department plans to spin off the Federal Student Aid office by 2027 or that Elon Musk has announced plans to start Roadster production in 2028.
The reaction across the accounts was not uniform. Some users responding to the @RedState post questioned whether a new agency would solve the underlying problem or simply rebrand it. Others praised the move as a long-overdue step toward fiscal responsibility. The @FirstSquawk post drew a different kind of response, with users noting the history of missed deadlines on the Roadster and expressing skepticism about the 2028 target. Neither account engaged with the replies in its original post, and the posts themselves did not include any additional sourcing or documentation.
The student loan portfolio represents one point six trillion dollars in outstanding debt owed by forty-five million borrowers, according to the report. Any restructuring of that portfolio would have significant implications for the federal budget, for borrowers' credit, and for the broader higher education landscape. The report did not address how the new agency would be funded or how its leadership would be selected, leaving those questions for another day.
As of the posts' timestamps, neither the Education Department nor Tesla had issued a public statement confirming the claims. The accounts that carried the news did so without providing independent verification, and the underlying report relied on anonymous sources. The story continues to develop.
Our Take
The reaction to the student loan spinoff plan is a reminder that the fight over federal education spending is far from over. The Constitution does not authorize the federal government to run a student loan program, and the fact that it has done so for decades does not make it right. Spinning off the Federal Student Aid office is a step in the right direction, but conservatives should be clear-eyed about what it is: a reorganization, not a repeal. The department still exists, the debt still exists, and the taxpayers are still on the hook for one point six trillion dollars. The real goal should be ending the federal student loan program entirely and returning education to the states and the private sector. If the Trump administration is serious about dismantling the Education Department, it should not settle for a rebranding exercise. As for the Roadster announcement, it is a distraction from the serious work of governance, and conservatives should not be swayed by shiny objects when the fiscal future of the country is at stake.

The plan would reshape how forty-five million borrowers repay the one point six trillion dollars currently in the Education Department's portfolio of outstanding debts, the report stated. It would also raise additional legal complications around the future of the department, an agency President Donald Trump and Secretary Linda McMahon have repeatedly said they want to eliminate entirely.
